newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House to discuss taxation of trust preferreds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House to discuss taxation of trust preferreds.

text.p: The House Ways & Means Committee on Wednesday morning will discuss a proposal to remove the tax deductible status of trust preferred securities and bonds with maturities longer than 40 years.
The committee is scheduled to look into the issue as part of its hearing on the Clinton Administration's fiscal 1998 tax proposals.
Washington sources said Wednesday's hearings will consist of testimony by various experts on the merits and financial market impact of closing the tax loopholes.

"We remain steadfastly opposed to the substance of the proposals," said Arthur Hyde, managing director at Salomon Brothers Inc, in his prepared testimony on behalf of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association.
But Hyde said the trade group is pleased with the adminstration's efforts to reduce market uncertainty by specifying generally what date the proposals, if passed, would become effective.z

The adminstration has specified that the proposal would become effective for instruments issued after "the date of the first committee action," which Washington sources consider the first full-committee markup. This is not expected for several months, they noted.
Wall Street analyst said issuers may cease to issue additional trust preferred stock following that date in order to avoid losing tax benefits.
But one Washington lobbyist noted, "It is by no means certain the tax committee will even take up this proposal. If Congress decides not to act, the effective date won't make any difference."

Unlike traditional preferred stock, trust preferred securities are currently treated as debt, allowing corporations to deduct interest payments. Similar to preferred stock, trust preferreds are structured to allow issuers to defer interest payments for a certain period of time.

Hyde and other supporters of preserving the tax-deferred status of trust preferred securities argue that these securities fill an important void in a corporation's capital structure by providing a long-term, fixed-rate source of capital that is junior to all other debt but senior to all equity.
Hyde said,"traditional preferred stock, for a variety of reasons, is an expensive and relatively unattractive source of capital for most corporations."
The adminstration characterizes the tax deductibilty of trust preferred securities as a exploitation of regulatory ambiguity in the definition of equity and debt instruments.
Because of their equity-like features, the adminstration has proposed removing interest deductibility for trust preferred securities as well as for debt with maturities longer than 40 years.

Wall Street analysts noted that based on current price levels, the financial markets are assuming that any tax change will not apply retroactively to the roughly $30 billion in outstanding trust preferred securities.
The Ways & Means hearing will be held in Washington at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
